sermons.life_context: Newly settled as pastor of New Park Street Chapel, Southwark, having accepted its call in April 1854 after his village pastorate at Waterbeach near Cambridge. His crowds led the church to hold services at Exeter Hall in early 1855 while the chapel was enlarged. This sermon began the regular weekly publication of his sermons, the series later known as the New Park Street Pulpit.

Pastor of New Park Street Chapel, Southwark, he preached this two days before marrying Susannah Thompson there on 8 January 1856. It fell on the sixth anniversary of his conversion in a Primitive Methodist chapel in Colchester; in the opening he says he heard this text preached that day, and his Autobiography's compilers cite that statement to fix the conversion date.

Pastor of New Park Street Chapel and living in the New Kent Road, he had married Susannah Thompson that January. He later dated his first ministerial student, the start of the Pastors' College, to 1856. The congregation's first service in the Surrey Gardens Music Hall followed on 19 October.

His first sermon after the Surrey Gardens Music Hall panic of 19 October 1856, in which seven people died at his congregation's first evening service there; the church book records that he was prostrated for some days. His twin sons had been born on 20 September. In the opening he said the instigators of the disturbance had his forgiveness.

Pastor of New Park Street Chapel, he was holding the church's Sunday-morning services in the Surrey Gardens Music Hall, begun on 23 November 1856 after the October disaster ended evening meetings there. He had married Susannah Thompson in January 1856, and their twin sons were born that September.

Pastor of New Park Street Chapel, whose Sunday-morning services were then held in the Surrey Gardens Music Hall, he came to the Crystal Palace for the national fast day after the Indian rebellion, less than a year after the Surrey Gardens disaster. By his own account this was his largest congregation in any building, and afterwards he slept from Wednesday night until Friday morning.

Pastor of New Park Street Chapel, he was preaching on Sunday mornings in the Surrey Gardens Music Hall, living in Nightingale Lane, Clapham, and had begun training ministers. By his own account the 'violent, rigid school of Hyper-Calvinists' condemned this sermon as Arminian, while he believed no other sermon of his had led to so many conversions.

Two weeks after 'Compel Them to Come In', he was still pastor of New Park Street Chapel, preaching Sunday mornings in the Surrey Gardens Music Hall and living in Nightingale Lane, Clapham. In the opening he ties this sermon to his previous two Sundays of preaching to the unconverted, answering whether such preaching promotes morality.

Pastor of the church that had met at New Park Street Chapel, Southwark, and living at Helensburgh House, Nightingale Lane, Clapham, he preached this a week after the new Metropolitan Tabernacle opened with a prayer meeting on 18 March 1861. The church cleared the remaining debt on 29 March and began regular Sunday worship in the building on 31 March.

Pastor of the Metropolitan Tabernacle, Newington, which had opened that March, he was living at Helensburgh House, Nightingale Lane, Clapham. The sermon refers to the recent collision in the Clayton tunnel (25 August 1861, 23 killed), and a CCEL editor's note also links it to a Kentish Town rail crash on 2 September.

He was in his first year at the new Metropolitan Tabernacle, Newington, living in Nightingale Lane, Clapham. The sermon came a month after the U.S. Navy took two Confederate envoys off the British ship Trent, a crisis the U.S. State Department's historians say raised the possibility of Anglo-American war; its references to war between two Christian nations fit that moment.

He was three years into his pastorate at the Metropolitan Tabernacle, Newington, and living in Nightingale Lane, Clapham. The sermon provoked a public controversy: by his own account he expected it to ruin sales of his printed sermons, which instead rose, and he withdrew from the Evangelical Alliance after its secretary wrote that he must retract or withdraw, a letter he later learned was unauthorized.
Pastor of the Metropolitan Tabernacle, Newington, he was living at Helensburgh House, Nightingale Lane, Clapham, and had launched his monthly magazine, The Sword and the Trowel, the previous year.

Pastor of the Metropolitan Tabernacle and living in Nightingale Lane, Clapham, he had by now launched The Sword and the Trowel (1865) and founded the Stockwell Orphanage (1867). A few weeks after this sermon, in November 1869, he fell ill with smallpox, though not in its worst form, shortly after attending the Lord Mayor's banquet on 9 November.

Pastor of the Metropolitan Tabernacle and head of its college and orphanage, he preached this in August 1880, the month his Autobiography gives for his move from Helensburgh House, Nightingale Lane, Clapham, to 'Westwood' on Beulah Hill, Upper Norwood; it does not give the day. He had been taking winter rests at Menton since at least early 1874.

sources.label: C. H. Spurgeon's Autobiography, ch. LXXXVII 'Westwood', p. 51 (The Spurgeon Library scan)

sermons.life_context: He was pastor of the Metropolitan Tabernacle, living at 'Westwood', Upper Norwood, where he had moved in 1880. The 'Down-grade' articles had begun appearing in his magazine The Sword and the Trowel that March; the controversy led to his withdrawal from the Baptist Union in October 1887.

Illness, recorded in his Autobiography as congestion of the lungs, had stopped his preaching in May 1891; he says in the sermon he chose the text partly because he was glad to meet his Lord in public again. It proved his last at the Tabernacle: his illness then became so serious that his death was feared, and he died at Menton on 31 January 1892.
